newsitem.title: USA: NFL AMERICAN FOOTBALL-LEAGUE'S SMALL TOWN TEAM OF GREEN BAY TOUCHES FANS.
newsitem.headline: NFL AMERICAN FOOTBALL-LEAGUE'S SMALL TOWN TEAM OF GREEN BAY TOUCHES FANS.

text.p: The small town team in football is back on top and headed for the Super Bowl and an audience of some 800 million television viewers and 42 million radio listeners.

The Green Bay Packers, representing a community of less than 200,000 on a Lake Michigan bay, return to the NFL's championship game for the first time in 29 years when they take on the New England Patriots next Sunday in New Orleans.

"Part of the charm, part of the appeal of this franchise is the size of the community and the well-documented loyalty and support from their fans," says Lee Remmell, the team's director of public relations, who covered the Packers as a sports writer for nearly 30 years before joining the team.

The team has sold out all seats at no-frills, 60,790-seat Lambeau Field on a season-ticket basis since 1960 despite having only five seasons with a winning record in the 25 years prior to the arrival of current coach Mike Holmgren in 1992.
"That is an incredible show of loyalty, I think, and support," said Remmell of the fans, many of whom wear "Cheesehead" hats to celebrate the area's dairy industry.

The team is unique in major U.S. sport, as it is owned by the community. The bond between the team and the town is indeed special, and can be seen on the field where the recent craze has Packer players leaping into the seats behind the end zone after scoring touchdowns to be hugged by adoring fans.
Longtime fan Angela Leatherman, 28, of Green Bay did not get to attend a game in person until obtaining a coveted ticket to Lambeau Field last season.

"A friend got a ticket for me when we played the Bears and we won the game," Leatherman said. "Then as a special treat, she was able to get me onto the field after the game. She told me to just walk across the field and enjoy the experience.

"But when I got to the 50-yard line, something just came over me and I dropped down, did a push-up and kissed our big Packers 'G' in the middle of the field. A police officer came up to me, but my friend had some influence and kept me from being arrested.

"My friend has refused to get me a ticket since, but it's okay, because I was actually there, first in the stadium and then even on the field, and I kissed our 'G'. I think I'll die happy because of that."
Affection for the team spreads beyond the borders of Wisconsin.
Despite their long absence from the Super Bowl, the Pack has maintained a popularity spawned by great championship teams under legendary coach Vince Lombardi in the 1960s.
Green Bay can even lay claim to capturing the title of "America's Team" from the Dallas Cowboys, as Packers' paraphernalia recently surpassed the Cowboys' in sales.
But it is in Green Bay where the NFL has what has been described as 'a pro city with a college atmosphere.'

"The players are so largely responsible for the affection the fans have for this team," said Duane Swift of the Green Bay Visitors and Convention Bureau. "And I equate it to the fact the town is so small.

"For instance, when you meet a movie star, and they take the time to shake your hand, you're more likely to have a favourable impression of that person. And these players by virtue of the fact it's such a small town, have touched everybody here.

"First of all, they actually have more of an opportunity to 'touch everybody' just by going to the store, or to the cleaners, to a movie or a mall, or to a gas station. Not just by jumping into the stands on a Sunday afternoon."
